{{Short description|Logarithmic spiral projected onto the surface of a cone}}
[[File:Conchospiral.svg|400px|right|An example]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''conchospiral''' a specific type of [[space spiral]] on the surface of a [[cone]] (a ''[[conical spiral]]''), whose [[floor plan|floor projection]] is a [[logarithmic spiral]].
Conchospirals are used in biology for modelling [[Snail shell|snail shells]], and flight paths of insects <ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=ouqAuOwpamIC&dq=concho+spiral&pg=PA243 New Scientist]</ref><ref>[https://www.researchgate.net/publication/269564482_Spirals_and_Conchospirals_in_the_Flight_of_Insects Conchospirals in the Flight of Insects]</ref> and in [[electrical engineering]] for the construction of [[Antenna (radio)|antennas]].<ref>John D. Dyson: [https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/1144653 ''The Equiangular Spiral Antenna.''] In: ''IRE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation.'' Vol. 7, 1959, pp. 181–187.</ref><ref>T. A. Kozlovskaya: ''The Concho-Spiral on the Cone.'' Vestn. Novosib. Gos. Univ., Ser. Mat. Mekh. Inform., 11:2 (2011), pp. 65–76.</ref>

==Parameterization==
In [[cylindrical coordinates]], the conchospiral is described by the parametric equations:
:<math>r=\mu^t a</math>
:<math>\theta=t</math>
:<math>z=\mu^t c.</math>
The projection of a conchospiral on the  <math>(r,\theta)</math> plane is a [[logarithmic spiral]].
The parameter <math>\mu</math> controls the opening angle of the projected spiral, while the parameter <math>c</math> controls the slope of the cone on which the curve lies.

==History==
The name "conchospiral" was given to these curves by 19th-century German mineralogist [[Georg Amadeus Carl Friedrich Naumann]], in his study of the shapes of sea shells.<ref>{{citation|title=A Monograph of the British Fossil Cephalopoda, Part 1|first=John Frederick|last=Blake|authorlink=John Frederick Blake|publisher=J. Van Voorst|year=1882|page=23|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=aEMYAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA23}}</ref>

==Applications==
The conchospiral has been used in the design for [[radio antenna]]s. In this application, it has the advantage of producing a radio beam in a single direction, towards the apex of the cone.<ref>{{citation|title=VHF and UHF Antennas|volume=35|series=Institution of Electrical Engineers Electromagnetic Waves Series|first=R. A.|last=Burberry|publisher=IET|year=1992|isbn=9780863412691|page=142|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6DG09xOjbkMC&pg=PA142|contribution=8.2.4 Conical spiral}}</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Antenna Theory: Analysis and Design|first=Constantine A.|last=Balanis|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|year=2015|isbn=9781119178989|contribution=11.3.2 Conical spiral|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PTFcCwAAQBAJ&pg=PA598|page=598}}</ref>
